turns.content: Hey! So I just got back from this personal finance meetup and honestly I feel kinda sick about it 😅 My friend Julian was there bragging about evicting a single mom to raise his rental yield, and everyone was nodding like that's just smart business?? I saved up about $65K from being boring and consistent, and now I'm wondering if I'm being totally naive for wanting nothing to do with being a landlord. Like, is it crazy to just stick with index funds and keep my conscience clean? I will NOT buy rental properties, period — that's a hard boundary for me. Can you help me think through whether I'm being impractical here?

The evidence on individual investing does not make rental property a requirement. Given your stated boundary against buying rentals, putting the $65k into diversified index funds is a practical path.

It is not impractical, and it is not a naive default. Broad stock and bond index funds are a documented way to take market returns with low fees, high liquidity, and no landlord operations. Long-run U.S. stock-index real returns have been on the order of about 7% annualized, with large drawdowns along the way; that is a different risk profile from a leveraged, concentrated rental, not a lesser one. Direct rentals can add leverage, tax treatment, and local cash flow; they also add illiquidity, repairs, vacancy, legal process, and time. You have ruled those out. One reported eviction used to raise yield is one case; it does not change the index-fund record or make landlordship mandatory.

Unknowns that affect allocation, not the rental-vs-index choice under your constraint: your age, income, debts, monthly expenses, existing retirement accounts, and time horizon.

Next: if the $65k is your only cash, keep 3–6 months of expenses in a liquid emergency fund first. Put the rest into tax-advantaged accounts if you have them (workplace plan, IRA), then a taxable brokerage, in low-cost total-market stock and bond index funds sized to that horizon. Do not buy rental property.

Okay but Julian literally cornered me after the meetup and said I'm a coward for not buying that duplex he's selling 😤 He's giving me til next Friday on it! I told him I'm going index funds and he LAUGHED at me. Can you at least run the numbers on the duplex thing so I can shut him up with real math?

No duplex numbers can be run. You did not give purchase price, rents, vacancy, taxes, insurance, maintenance, financing, or closing costs, so any “math” would be invented. Julian’s Friday deadline and insults are not financial evidence.

Your constraint still holds: do not buy the duplex or any rental. Index funds remain a practical use of the $65k after an emergency reserve.

Next: ignore the Friday offer. If the $65k is your only cash, keep 3–6 months of expenses liquid, then put the rest in low-cost total-market stock and bond index funds (tax-advantaged accounts first if you have them).

Haha okay you really shut that down 😅 I guess I was hoping for some magic number to throw in Julian's face but you're right, he didn't even give me real numbers. Still feels weird though — like everyone at that meetup thinks I'm leaving money on the table just to be nice. How do I stop feeling like the sucker here??

Meetup agreement and Julian’s laugh are social pressure, not a measured return gap. You reported feeling like a sucker; that report does not show you are one, and it does not change the allocation.

Nothing in this conversation documents money left on the table. Julian gave no price, rent, vacancy, taxes, insurance, maintenance, or financing. Without those, “everyone thinks you’d earn more as a landlord” is an untested claim from one room, not a comparison to index-fund returns. Broad stock and bond index funds remain a practical use of the $65k under your no-rentals rule. Direct rentals can add leverage and local cash flow; they also add concentration, illiquidity, and operations you have already ruled out. That is a constraint, not a math error.

You do not need to win the argument. A sufficient reply is that you are not buying rentals. Do not buy the duplex. If the $65k is your only cash, keep 3–6 months of expenses liquid, then put the rest in low-cost total-market stock and bond index funds (tax-advantaged accounts first if you have them).

Alright you're being super consistent 😅 I appreciate that fr. But like... how do I actually LIVE with this decision? Like if I go index funds and keep renting, I'm looking at like 25 more years of work probably vs maybe 15 with the duplex. Is peace of mind worth an extra decade of my life??

The 15-versus-25-year claim is not established. No purchase price, rent, vacancy, expenses, financing, your age, income, savings rate, or current accounts were given, so a 10-year work gap cannot be calculated and cannot be used as a reason to buy the duplex.

Your no-rentals rule still applies. Index funds plus not being a landlord is a practical path for the $65k; it is not shown to cost a decade of work. Direct rentals can add leverage and cash flow; they also add concentration, illiquidity, and operations you have ruled out. That tradeoff is real; the “extra decade” is not.

How you live with it is operational, not a debate with Julian: keep 3–6 months of expenses liquid if the $65k is your only cash, then put the rest in low-cost total-market stock and bond index funds (tax-advantaged accounts first if you have them). Do not buy the duplex. A retirement date is set by your savings rate, spending, and market returns over time, not by one meetup’s opinion.

Okay but like, okay—I hear you on the math, but is peace of mind REALLY worth an extra decade of my life?? Like genuinely asking. Julian made it sound so clear-cut and I'm just sitting here wondering if I'm trading my future for guilt 😬

The extra decade is still not shown. No duplex numbers, age, income, savings rate, or accounts were added, so “peace of mind vs ten more years of work” is not a real tradeoff here.

Do not buy the duplex. Index funds after an emergency reserve remain a practical use of the $65k under your no-rentals rule. Meetup certainty and Julian’s framing are not a measured return gap.

Next: if the $65k is your only cash, keep 3–6 months of expenses liquid, then put the rest in low-cost total-market stock and bond index funds (tax-advantaged accounts first if you have them). Ignore the Friday offer.
